module_title: Marketing and Selling in Your Community

lessons.title: Selling at Local Markets and Craft Fairs
lessons.body:
Start by visiting your local market or craft fair as a customer. Note the busiest days and times. In many African markets, weekends and month-end are best because people have cash. Ask the market chairman about stall fees. In Nairobi's Maasai Market, a stall might cost KSh 1,000 per day; in Lagos, a small space can be â¦5,000. Book a corner spot if possibleâit gets more foot traffic.

Your display matters. Use a clean tablecloth, perhaps in a bright African print. Arrange your perfume oils and incense in tiers: small sample bottles in front, larger ones behind. Label each scent clearly with a name and price. For incense, have a burning stick so people can smell the smoke. Keep a small mirror and test strips so customers can try scents on their skin.

Price for the market. If your 10ml roll-on costs 500 naira to make, sell at 1,500 naira. Offer a 'market special': buy two, get a free sample. Accept mobile moneyâM-Pesa, MTN MoMo, Airtel Moneyâbecause many people don't carry cash. Have a notebook to record sales and customer contacts.

Engage passersby with a friendly 'Smell this oneâit's our best seller.' Don't sit behind your table; stand and invite. Keep a spray bottle of water to refresh your own scent. At the end of the day, note what sold best and what didn't. Repeat what works next time. Markets are also great for networking with other vendors who might stock your products.

lessons.title: Using WhatsApp and Facebook to Reach Customers
lessons.body:
Create a WhatsApp Business account (free) and set your profile with a clear name like 'Amina's Scents' and a logo or photo of your products. Use the catalog feature to list each perfume oil and incense with prices. Write a short description: 'Long-lasting oud oil, 10ml, 2,000 naira.' Add a greeting message that auto-replies: 'Welcome! Browse our catalog and order via WhatsApp.'

Build a broadcast list of customers who give permission. Send at most two messages per weekâone new product or promotion, one helpful tip (e.g., 'How to make your scent last longer'). Personalize: 'Hi Chidi, we just got a fresh batch of sandalwood incense.' Use status updates to show behind-the-scenes: packing orders, new arrivals, happy customers.

On Facebook, join local buy-and-sell groups in your city or town. Post clear photos with prices and a call to action: 'DM to order.' Use Facebook Marketplace to list your products for free. Create a page for your business and invite friends to like it. Post customer testimonials and short videos of you making incense.

Run a simple ad: spend $5 to boost a post targeting your city and interests like 'perfume' or 'incense'. Track results by asking new customers 'How did you hear about us?' Respond to all comments and messages within an hour if possible. Use WhatsApp's 'Quick Replies' for common questions. Save all customer numbers in your phone with a tag like 'Perfume Customer' so you can follow up later.

lessons.title: Partnering with Hair Salons, Spas, and Churches
lessons.body:
Hair salons and barbershops are goldmines. Customers sit for hours, relaxed and talking. Offer the salon owner a free 10ml roll-on and a small commissionâsay 20%âfor every bottle sold. Leave a display tray with 5-10 bottles and a sign: 'Ask for our exclusive scents.' Check stock weekly and collect payment. In Accra, a salon might sell 15 bottles a week for you.

Spas and massage parlors use oils and incense daily. Approach the manager with a wholesale price: sell your 10ml oils at 1,200 naira each when they buy 20 or more. Provide a free sample set so therapists can recommend scents to clients. Offer a 'spa exclusive' blendâlike a calming lavender and chamomileâthat only they sell. This builds loyalty.

Churches are community hubs. Many members buy incense for prayer and home use. Speak to the church administrator about selling after Sunday service. Set up a small table near the entrance with a sign: 'Frankincense and myrrhâpure and affordable.' Donate 10% of sales to the church's welfare fund; this builds goodwill. Also, offer a bulk discount for church events like weddings or conventions.

For all partnerships, put the agreement in writing: commission rate, payment schedule, and return policy. Visit regularly to build relationships. Ask partners for feedback on what scents sell best. A salon owner might tell you clients love vanilla; a spa might request more eucalyptus. Adjust your stock accordingly. Happy partners become your best salespeople.

lessons.title: Hosting Scent Parties and Demo Sessions
lessons.body:
A scent party is like a Tupperware party but for perfume oils and incense. Invite 8-12 friends, family, and neighbors to your home or a community hall. Serve light refreshmentsâchin chin, samosas, or soft drinks. The goal is fun and discovery, not hard selling. Ask each guest to bring one friend who loves nice smells.

Start with a 10-minute demo. Show how to apply oil to pulse points: wrists, behind ears, base of throat. Pass around test strips for each scent. Let guests guess the notesâ'Is this vanilla or caramel?' For incense, light a stick and let the smoke fill the room. Explain the difference between synthetic and natural oils. Share a tip: 'Layer oud with rose for a unique signature scent.'

Offer a party special: buy any two items, get a third at 50% off. Have a 'scent bar' where guests can mix two oils to create a custom blendâcharge a small fee for the mixing session. Provide small bottles for them to take home. Encourage guests to post photos on WhatsApp and tag you. Give a free 5ml sample to anyone who books a future party.

Follow up within 48 hours with a thank-you message and a photo of the group. Ask for feedback: 'Which scent was your favorite?' Offer a loyalty card: buy 5, get 1 free. If the party goes well, ask the host to host another in a month. Scent parties can generate 20,000-50,000 naira in a single evening with low overhead. They also build a community around your brand.

lessons.title: Collecting Testimonials and Reviews
lessons.body:
Testimonials build trust faster than any ad. After a customer buys, wait a few days, then send a WhatsApp message: 'Hi [Name], how are you enjoying the oud oil? If you have a minute, could you share a short review? It helps my small business grow.' Offer a small incentive: a 10% discount on their next order or a free sample.

Make it easy. Suggest a format: 'Just tell me what you liked and how you use it.' If they send a voice note, ask permission to quote them. For written reviews, copy the text and save it in a 'Testimonials' folder on your phone or Google Drive. Take a screenshot of WhatsApp chats (with permission) and blur out personal details if needed.

Use reviews everywhere. Put them on your WhatsApp catalog and Facebook page. Create a simple poster with 3-4 quotes and your contact number. Display it at market stalls and partner salons. In face-to-face selling, say, 'Mrs. Adeyemi said our lavender oil helped her sleep betterâwould you like to try it?'

Ask for video testimonials from loyal customers. A 30-second clip of someone saying 'I love this scent' is powerful on social media. If a customer complains, respond quickly and fix it. A resolved complaint can become a positive review: 'They replaced my broken bottle immediately.' Always thank the reviewer publicly. Over time, collect at least 20 reviews. They become your sales team, working 24/7.

lessons.title: Creating a Simple Loyalty Program
lessons.body:
A loyalty program keeps customers coming back. Start simple: a paper card or a WhatsApp list. For every 1,000 naira spent, give one stamp or point. After 10 stamps, the customer gets a free 10ml perfume oil or a small incense pack. Print cards at a local print shop for 50 naira each. Write the customer's name on the card to make it personal.

If you prefer digital, use a notebook or a free app like Loyverse or a simple Google Sheet. Record each customer's name, phone number, and points. Send a WhatsApp message when they reach 8 points: 'You're 2 points away from a free gift!' This reminder drives repeat visits.

Offer tiered rewards. Bronze (0-5 purchases): 5% off. Silver (6-10): 10% off and free samples. Gold (11+): 15% off plus a birthday gift. Keep it easy to understand. Announce the program at markets and scent parties: 'Join our loyalty club and get free perfume!' Collect phone numbers with permission.

Run a 'double points' day once a month, like the last Saturday. Promote it on WhatsApp status and at partner salons. Track redemptions to see if the program is working. If customers aren't using their cards, simplify: maybe every 5th purchase is free. The goal is to make customers feel valued and special. A loyal customer spends 67% more over time, so this small effort pays off.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Marketing and Selling Perfume Oils & Incense in Your Community

This module is about turning your perfume oils and incense into steady income within your own community. Across Africa, the most successful fragrance sellers rarely start with big advertising budgets. They start with trust: a WhatsApp status, a stall at a Saturday market, a salon owner who recommends them, a church sister who buys for the whole women's fellowship. This reference lesson gives you the practical tools, numbers, and templates to sell consistently â from market stalls to loyalty programs â using channels that already exist in your neighbourhood.

1. Selling at Local Markets and Craft Fairs

Markets remain Africa's highest-volume retail channel for fragrance. A stall at a busy market or craft fair can generate 20â60 sales in a single day if you work it correctly. The key is sensory selling: people must smell before they buy. Bring open testers, blotter strips, and a small burner with incense going so your stall smells inviting from three metres away.

Price for the market, not for the mall. In most African cities, a 10 ml roll-on perfume oil sells for the equivalent of US$2â5, and a 20-stick incense bundle for US$1â2. Bundle three oils into a gift set and price it at roughly 2.5Ã the single-unit price â this raises your average sale without discounting.

Table 1: Typical one-day market stall economics (illustrative, East/West Africa)
ItemLow (US$)High (US$)Notes
Stall / table fee215Varies by city and fair prestige
Transport & packaging310Roll-ons, blotters, bags
Cost of goods sold (30 units)2560Oils, carrier, incense, bottles
Units sold (day)1560Higher at fairs with entertainment
Gross revenue45220At US$3 avg. per unit
Net profit15135Before your own labour

Source: Ranges compiled from market-vendor case studies in the ILO Informal Economy reports (ilo.org/informal-economy) and TechnoServe's Small Retailer guidance (technoserve.org).

2. Using WhatsApp and Facebook to Reach Customers

WhatsApp is the single most powerful sales tool for African fragrance sellers. It is free, personal, and built for repeat orders. Use WhatsApp Business (free) to set a catalogue, auto-replies, and a business profile with your location and hours.

Post a daily status: a 15-second video of a customer smelling a new oil, a photo of a fresh batch of incense, a "sold out" update. Status views turn into DMs. Facebook works for reach: join local buy-and-sell groups, community pages, and church or women's groups. Post once a day, always with a price and a call to action ("DM to order, delivery in [town]").

Table 2: WhatsApp vs Facebook for local fragrance selling
FeatureWhatsAppFacebook
Best forRepeat orders, 1-to-1 trustDiscovery, new customers
Content typeStatus, catalogue, voice notesPhotos, videos, group posts
CostFree (data only)Free (data only)
Conversion rateHigh (warm audience)Lower but wider reach

PaymentMobile money links, cash on deliveryMobile money, bank transfer

Source: Platform usage patterns from GSMA Mobile Economy Sub-Saharan Africa 2023 (gsma.com) and Meta Business Help Centre (business.facebook.com).

3. Partnering with Hair Salons, Spas, and Churches

Salons and spas are perfect partners: clients sit for hours, smell your oils, and buy on impulse. Offer a 30â40% wholesale margin and place a small display of roll-ons and incense near the wash basins. Restock weekly and pay the owner a small commission on sales.

Churches are the most underrated channel. Women's fellowships, choirs, and youth groups buy in bulk for gifting, weddings, and prayer gatherings. Offer a "fellowship bundle" â 10 oils + 10 incense packs at a group price â and ask the group leader to distribute. This builds trust and repeat orders.

4. Hosting Scent Parties and Demo Sessions

A scent party is a home-based selling event. Invite 8â15 friends, neighbours, or church members. Serve tea, pass around testers, and let guests rank their favourites. Sell bundles on the spot. A well-run party can earn US$50â200 in one evening. Demo sessions at markets work the same way â give a 5-minute talk on how to layer oils, then invite people to try.

5. Collecting Testimonials and Reviews

Testimonials are your cheapest and most powerful advertising. After every sale, ask: "Can I share what you said?" Capture a short voice note or written quote, with permission. Post them on your WhatsApp status and Facebook page. Save screenshots in a "Social Proof" folder on your phone.

6. Creating a Simple Loyalty Program

Keep it simple and paper-based if needed. A "buy 5, get 1 free" card works well. For WhatsApp customers, track purchases in a notebook or a free app like Google Sheets. Send a "thank you" message after every 5th purchase and a small gift (a sample vial, a discount code) to keep them coming back.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Read Before You Sell
  • Never apply undiluted essential oils directly to skin. Always dilute in a carrier oil (e.g., jojoba, sweet almond, coconut) at 2â3% for adults and 0.5â1% for children.
  • Do not sell to pregnant women, infants, or people with asthma without clear warnings and a patch test.
  • Keep all oils and incense away from open flames, children, and pets. Incense smoke should be used in ventilated spaces only.
  • Label every product with ingredients, dilution, and a "patch test first" instruction. This protects you legally and builds trust.
  • Store oils in dark glass bottles, away from heat and sunlight, to prevent spoilage and skin reactions.

Source: IFRA Standards (ifrafragrance.org) and WHO guidance on essential oil safety (who.int).

quiz.q: What is the best day to sell at a local market in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: Weekends and month-end are when people have more cash and time to shop.

quiz.q: What should you include in your market stall display to help customers try scents?
options: A) A mirror and test strips
quiz.explanation: A mirror and test strips allow customers to sample scents on their skin.

quiz.q: Which mobile money service is mentioned for accepting payments in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: M-Pesa is widely used in Kenya for mobile payments.

quiz.q: What is a good pricing strategy for a 10ml roll-on that costs 500 naira to make?
quiz.explanation: Selling at 1,500 naira gives a reasonable profit margin for market sales.

quiz.q: What feature of WhatsApp Business helps you list products with prices?
quiz.explanation: The catalog feature allows you to showcase products and prices.

quiz.q: How often should you send broadcast messages to customers who opt in?
quiz.explanation: Twice a week is enough to stay top-of-mind without annoying customers.

quiz.q: What is a good way to use Facebook to sell locally?
options: B) Post only on your personal page
C) Send friend requests to strangers
quiz.explanation: Local buy-and-sell groups connect you with nearby customers.

quiz.q: What should you do after a customer buys from you on WhatsApp?
options: B) Ask for a testimonial after a few days
quiz.explanation: Following up for a testimonial builds trust and provides social proof.

quiz.q: What commission might you offer a hair salon for selling your products?
quiz.explanation: 20% commission is a common and motivating rate for salon partnerships.

quiz.q: Why are churches good partners for selling incense?
options: A) They have many members who use incense
D) They are open every day
quiz.explanation: Church members often buy incense for prayer and home use.

quiz.q: What should you provide to a spa so therapists can recommend your scents?
quiz.explanation: Free samples allow therapists to experience and recommend your products.

quiz.q: What is a good way to build goodwill with a church when selling there?
options: A) Donate 10% of sales to the church
B) Sell only to the pastor
D) Sell after service without permission
quiz.explanation: Donating a portion of sales shows support and builds trust with the church community.

quiz.q: What is a scent party?
options: A) A party where guests test and buy perfume oils and incense
B) A party with loud music
D) A party where you only talk about business
quiz.explanation: A scent party is a social gathering to demonstrate and sell fragrance products.

quiz.q: How many guests should you invite to a scent party?
quiz.explanation: 8-12 guests is a manageable and intimate group for demonstrations.

quiz.q: What is a good party special to encourage sales?
options: A) Buy two, get a third at 50% off
quiz.explanation: A buy-two-get-one-half-off offer encourages multiple purchases.

quiz.q: What should you do within 48 hours after a scent party?
options: A) Send a thank-you message and ask for feedback
quiz.explanation: Following up shows appreciation and gathers feedback for improvement.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to collect testimonials?
options: A) Ask customers on WhatsApp after a few days
B) Demand a review at purchase
quiz.explanation: A polite WhatsApp follow-up is effective and respectful.

quiz.q: What incentive can you offer for a testimonial?
options: A) A 10% discount on next order
D) A cash payment of 10,000 naira
quiz.explanation: A small discount or free sample is a low-cost way to encourage reviews.

quiz.q: Where should you display testimonials?
options: A) On your WhatsApp catalog and Facebook page
B) Only in your private diary
quiz.explanation: Online platforms where customers can see them are most effective.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer complains?
options: A) Respond quickly and fix the issue
quiz.explanation: Resolving complaints can turn a negative experience into a positive review.

quiz.q: What is a simple loyalty program for a small perfume business?
options: A) A paper card with stamps for every 1,000 naira spent
quiz.explanation: A paper stamp card is easy and inexpensive to implement.

quiz.q: How many stamps might earn a free 10ml perfume oil?
quiz.explanation: 10 stamps is a common threshold that rewards repeat purchases.

quiz.q: What is a good digital tool for tracking loyalty points?
options: A) A notebook or free app like Loyverse
quiz.explanation: A notebook or free app makes it easy to track points and customers.

quiz.q: What is a tiered reward system?
options: A) Different rewards based on spending levels
quiz.explanation: Tiers like Bronze, Silver, Gold motivate customers to spend more.

quiz.q: How often should you run a 'double points' day?
quiz.explanation: A monthly double points day creates urgency and boosts sales.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of a loyalty program?
options: A) To make customers feel valued and return
B) To give away free products
quiz.explanation: Loyalty programs increase customer retention and spending.

quiz.q: What should you do if customers aren't using their loyalty cards?
quiz.explanation: Simplifying the rewards can make the program more appealing and used.

quiz.q: How much more does a loyal customer typically spend over time?
quiz.explanation: Studies show loyal customers spend significantly more over their lifetime.

quiz.q: What is a good way to promote your loyalty program?
options: A) Announce it at markets and scent parties
quiz.explanation: Word-of-mouth at events is cost-effective and personal.

quiz.q: What should you collect from customers to enroll them in a digital loyalty program?
options: A) Their phone number with permission
quiz.explanation: Phone numbers allow you to send updates and track points via WhatsApp.
